messages.subject: sum percentages for each facet; requires "group", but "group" overwrites “fill”?
messages.subject_clean: sum percentages for each facet; requires "group", but "group" overwrites “fill”?
messages.body_plain:
I just posted this on Stackoverflow: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/12236160/ggplot-sum-percentages-for-each-facet-respect-fill

Basically, the code below doesn't respect fill - so it seems I can't give each bar a unique color AND have the bars sum to 100 for each facet?

ggplot(test, aes(test2)) +

     geom_bar(aes(y = ..density.., fill=test2,group=test1)) +

     facet_grid(~test1)

Example data:

test <- data.frame(

     test1 = sample(letters[1:2], 100, replace = TRUE),

     test2 = sample(letters[3:8], 100, replace = TRUE)

 )
Thanks in advance

Sincerely
Andreas

messages.subject: Re: Gradient colours with area
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, Sep 3, 2012 at 3:10 AM, Fabien Espic <fabien...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thanks for the answer.
> The code I wrote was hypothetical. It was just meaning "for the medium
> values, use the color yellow".
>
> So  there is no way to have an area with a gradient colour with ggplot2?

If what you want is a gradient within a geom_area, it's not possible
to do with ggplot2. ggplot2 is built on grid graphics, which I believe
doesn't support it.

-Winston

Am I missing something or is this a bug? The same happens with pdf() in windows and in linux.

Thanks

> On Monday, August 27, 2012 12:19:55 AM UTC+2, winston wrote:
>>
>> A few things about this:
>>
>> - It makes it much easier to see and diagnose problems if a simple
>> reproducible example is used. See the link at the bottom of these
>> mailing list messages for how to do this. If readers of the mailing
>> list can simply copy and paste the code, then they are much more
>> likely to help.
>>
>> - Presently the 'size' parameter is scaled so that the range of the
>> data is mapped (linearly) to the radius range 1 to 6. This means there
>> are two hurdles in making a balloon plot, where the area is
>> proportional to the value.
>> First, since the data range is mapped to the size/radius range, this
>> means that if your data goes from 1-6, those values get mapped to the
>> same size range as if the data goes from 20-40. The smallest data
>> values get mapped to size 1, and the largest data values get mapped to
>> size 6. This may seem counterintuitive, but it is the same way that
>> mappings work for, say, color gradients: the smallest data value is
>> mapped to the color on one end of the gradient, and the largest data
>> value is mapped to the color on the other end, no matter what the data
>> values are. This can be addressed by setting the limits and range for
>> the scale.
>> Second, since the values are mapped linearly with respect to radius,
>> even if you fix the first issue, there's still a problem. Suppose, for
>> convenience, that your data goes from 1-6. Then a data value of 6 will
>> be represented by a circle that's twice the radius for a data value of
>> 3 -- meaning it will be 4x the area. Using scale_area will address
>> this issue.
>>
>> - The presence of the decimal points in the legend is not necessarily
>> a bug. stat_sum calculates numeric values. Even though the values for
>> that particular stat are always integers, to the rest of ggplot2, they
>> are simply values on a continuous (as opposed to discrete) scale. It
>> uses the same break-calculation algorithm as it does for any other
>> continuous values, and the result is that if the range is 1-4, it
>> generates a legend that includes 0.5 steps. In other words, the
>> generality of ggplot2 involves some trade-offs - you get more
>> flexibility, but it may not be as good for every particular case. At
>> any rate, the way to make it not display decimal points is to use
>> something like breaks=1:4 in the scale.
>>
>>
>> -Winston

messages.subject: Re: editGrob on a ggplotGrob returned object
messages.subject_clean: editGrob on a ggplotGrob returned object
messages.body_plain:
g is a gtable object. You can inspect it with the following:

# Show the structure of the gtable object, but don't recurse into sub-components
str(g, max.level=1)

# Print the data frame recording layout
g$layout

# Get the list of grobs in the gtable
g$grobs

# Get a 1x1 gtable that contains just the title
g[2,4]

This code will have the effect you're looking for. It might be worth
thinking about how to modify the gtable API to make this sort of
access easier.

library(ggplot2)
library(grid)
library(gtable)
p <- qplot(wt, mpg, data = mtcars, colour = cyl, main = "Title text")
g <- ggplotGrob(p)

# Get index of the title grob
idx <- which(g$layout$name == "title")

# Modify the title grob and save it back
g$grobs[[idx]] <- editGrob(g$grobs[[idx]], gp = gpar(fontface =
"italic", col="red"))

grid.draw(g)

It would also be nice to be able to do something like grid.ls <http://grid.ls>() on a
gtable and get back a useful result.

-Winston

splitString <- function (text, width)
{
  if(is.null(text)) return(NULL)
  strings <- strsplit(text, " ")[[1]]
  newstring <- strings[1]
  linewidth <- stringWidth(newstring)
  gapwidth <- stringWidth(" ")
  availwidth <- convertWidth(width, "inches", valueOnly = TRUE)
  for (i in 2:length(strings)) {
    width <- stringWidth(strings[i])
        if (convertWidth(linewidth + gapwidth + width, "inches",
            valueOnly = TRUE) < availwidth) {
            sep <- " "
            linewidth <- linewidth + gapwidth + width
        }
        else {
            sep <- "\n"
            linewidth <- width
        }
        newstring <- paste(newstring, strings[i], sep = sep)
    }
  newstring
}

messages.body_plain:
There is a new theming system in 0.9.2 so some things that used to work in the old system might break in the new one. Plot titling is also affected in this version. The titling itself is moved out of opts() (now theme() in 0.9.2); one now generates plot titles either with the title = argument in labs() or with the new ggtitle() function. This is why Brandon's code works in 0.9.2.

Brandon's solution indicates that one can apply theme functions to individual theme elements in this version of ggplot2 (nice job, BTW!)  Although it works for now, theme_title() will have to be modified to conform to the new theming system in order to survive into future versions. I'll defer to Winston re commentary on applying theme functions to individual theme elements (e.g., plot.title) in the new system. I need to study theme_title and how it behaves in the new system.

A document is in preparation re the new theming system that should be available within the next week. I'm adding a few things to the current version and this example looks like something worth adding. After running it through the ggplot2-dev group for vetting, we'll put it up somewhere and make an announcement to the group.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Plots of backtransformed data
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

It's a little difficult to help since you didn't provide a reproducible example, but your question appears to have something to do with the distinction between scale transformations and coordinate transformations. Perhaps section 7.3 of
http://cloud.github.com/downloads/hadley/ggplot2/guide-col.pdf
might be of some assistance; if not, please provide a reproducible example (small data set + code) to make it easier for others to help. We don't have mydata2, nor do we know what is options1. If you provide a small data set, please use dput form to send it (see ?dput if this is news to you).

Stab in the dark:
Coordinate transformation is done after statistical transformation, so you should either not use transformed data in the initial ggplot() call or you should be using inverse transforms in coord_trans(). The example using the diamonds data in the cited section of the aforementioned document demonstrates what I mean.

Dennis

messages.subject_clean: Significance level added to matrix correlation in ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Hey, using the second example in SO.

ggplot(nbar.m, aes(x=row, y=variable, fill=value, alpha=valuep))+geom_tile()+scale_fill_gradientn(colours=c("red", "yellow", "green"))+theme_bw()+scale_alpha(na.value=0, range=c(1,0), guide=F)

Something like that.

I reversed the scale_alpha for the p-value so the more significant stuff shows up brighter. I know the colors suck, but you can pick whatever you want using scale_gradientn(). I also hid the legend for alpha. I still think you should adjust the scale for alpha to have >.90 = dark, .70<=x<.90 = middle, and so on... maybe instead of continuous scale, use cut() here to set the alpha more precisely.

Just an idea. What you need is something that you can look at and determine what's important. I happen to like the way this turned out (other than the colors being a bit too bright).

B

Hi,

I believe this to be an easy question, but I am stumped.

I have multiple measurements at set of locations. Without preprocessing it using plyr or aggregate, how would I set color or size to reflect the mean?

For example,

temp <- data.frame( x = rep(1:3, each = 3), y = rep(1:3, each = 3), value = rnorm(9))

messages.subject: ggplot2 0.9.2 released
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -

ggplot2 0.9.2 has been released! The source and binary versions should
be available on the CRAN mirrors by now.

Your existing code should continue to work, although you may receive
warnings about functions that have been deprecated. Replacing them
with new versions is easy. Here are the changes you are likely to
encounter:

* opts() is deprecated. You can simply replace it with theme() in your code.

* theme_blank(), theme_text(), theme_rect(), theme_line(), and
theme_segment() are deprecated. You can replace them with
element_blank(), element_text(), element_rect(), and element_line().

* Previously, the way to set the title of a plot was opts(title="Title
text"). In the new version, use ggtitle("Title text") or
labs(title="Title text").

These functions were renamed so that the names would make more sense.

There are also a number of enhancements to the theming system that
make it easier to modify themes. If you'd like to learn more about
more about it, see:
  https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/wiki/New-theme-system

Dennis Murphy is also writing a detailed document on the new theme
system, which should be available in the next few weeks.

This version was the first to have a release candidate stage. The RC
was available for one month, but wasn't widely announced. For future
releases, we'll probably announce the release candidate on this
mailing list so that more users can test it out before the final
release.

Below is the list of changes in the NEWS file for ggplot2 0.9.2:

----------------------------------------------------------------

THEME SYSTEM

* The theme system has been completely rewritten. (Winston Chang)

* The functions `theme_text`, `theme_line`, and so on have been renamed to
  `element_text`, `element_line`, and so on.

* The `opts()` function has been renamed to `theme()`.

* To set the plot title, use `labs(title = "...")` or `ggtitle("...")
  instead of `opts(title = "...")`.

* Elements are now just lists of properties, instead of functions that
  return grobs.

* Theme elements now can inherit properties. For example, `axis.title.x`
  inherits properties from `axis.title`, which in turn inherits from
  `text`. The inheritance tree is stored in ggplot2::.element_tree.

* Theme objects can now be added to each other with `+`, without a ggplot
  object. There is also a new `%replace%` operator for adding theme
  objects together.

* Vertical and horizontal grid lines can now be controlled independently,
  with `axis.grid.major.x`, `axis.grid.major.y` (and the same for minor);
  `axis.ticks.x` and `axis.ticks.y`; and `axis.line.x` and `axis.line.y`.

* The `size` property of theme elements can be defined relative to the
  parent objects, using the `rel()` function.

MINOR FEATURES

* ggplot2 now uses the external gtable package instead of internal gtable
  functions.

* The condition that set parameters (e.g. `colour = "red"`) could only be of
  length one has been relaxed - they may now be of length one, or exactly the
  same length as the data. Recycling is not done because it makes it harder to
  spot problems. This makes `annotate` considerably more flexible. (Fixes
  #489)

* `stat_contour` is now somewhat faster

* new stat class `stat_ecdf` that shows empirical cumulative distribution
  function. (Kohske Takahashi)

* Dependency on `gpclib` removed, and `fortify.SpatialPolygonsDataFrame` will
  now use `rgeos` if available - this is particularly useful if you're not
  able to use the non-free `gpclib`.

* `ggsave` now supports emf output files.

* all "template" plots (`plotmatrix`, `ggorder` etc) have been deprecated and
  will be removed in a future version. These plots are poorly tested and
  poorly supported and really belong in a separate package.

* The default guide for continuous color/fill scale is now colourbar.
  (Kohske Takahashi. Fixes #555)

* The arrowhead of geom-path and geom-segment with `arrow = TRUE` is
  now filled with the same colour as the path.

* The algorithm for calculating breaks locations has been changed from
  `pretty_breaks()` to `extended_breaks()` from the 'labeling' package
  by Justin Talbot. (Winston Chang. Fixes #580)

* `scale_type`, the function used to pick which type of scale should be
   used for a given type of input variable is now an S3 generic. That
   means that if you want to add a new default type of scale you can
   provide a method - it should return a string giving the name of the
   scale to use (e.g. "continuous", "discrete", "date")

* When there are multiple guides (legends), the order that they are
  displayed can now be controlled manually. (Kohske Takahashi. Fixes
  #470)

* When a scale for a given aesthetic is added to a plot more than once,
  display a message indicating that the first scale will be replaced.
  (Winston Chang. Fixes #518)

DOCUMENTATION

* All geoms and stats now document their aesthetics. (Thanks to joranE.
  Fixes #447)

BUG FIXES

* `scale_x_continuous` now respects `na.value` (Fixes #522)

* `geom_map` now correctly uses set aesthetics (e.g. `colour = "green"`)

* Setting breaks outside the limits of the x or y axis no longer causes
  errors. (Kohske Takahashi. Fixes #552)

* `facet_locate` no longer evaluates unneeded expressions. (Winston
  Chang. Fixes #565)

* `annotation_map` now gets group id from munched data. (Winston Chang.
  Fixes #568)

* `geom_raster` now supports alpha. (Kohske Takahashi. Fixes #596)

* Both axis lines are now drawn above the plotting area panel.
  (Winston Chang. Fixes #585)

* The jitter resolution is now correctly calculated when the data
  does _not_ include zero. (Thanks to Karl Ove Hufthammer. Fixes #572)

* Legend icons for `geom_boxplot` now display linetype. (Kohske
  Takahashi. Fixes #608)

* Facets now appear in the correct order when layers with different
  factor levels are added. (Winston Chang. Fixes #543)

* Distances in polar coordinates are calculated along spiral arcs,
  instead of straight-line distance. (Winston Chang. Fixes #471)

* `fortify.SpatialPolygonsDataFrame` now uses the correct ordering.
  (Charlotte Wickham. Fixes #434)

* `stat_vline` and `stat_hline` no longer throw errors when
  `xintercept` and `yintercept` are passed to them. (Winston Chang.
  Fixes #624)

Here's one way to get the back-transformed fitted model in the original units of measurement.

library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# Base plot
p <- ggplot(dataset1, aes(x, y)) +
          geom_point(aes(shape = site), size = 4, alpha = 0.5)

# Rescale to log coordinates and fit the model
p1 <- p + scale_x_continuous(trans = "log") + scale_y_continuous(trans = "log") +
           geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm")

# Now back-transform using coord_trans():
p1 + coord_trans(x = "exp", y = "exp")

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Independent control over axis lines in 0.9.2
messages.subject_clean: Independent control over axis lines in 0.9.2
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Because of the inheritance structure built into the new theming system, the way to do it is to modify axis.line and then use element_blank() on axis.line.y:

baseplot +  theme(axis.line = element_line(colour = "red", linetype = "dashed", size = 1),
                           axis.line.y = element_blank())

axis.line.x will inherit from axis.line and you'll get the behavior you expect.

Dennis

messages.subject: Changing the symbol in the legend key in 0.9.2
messages.subject_clean: Changing the symbol in the legend key in 0.9.2
messages.body_plain:
When using an aesthetic in geom_text, the symbol that appears in the legend key is a lower case "a". Some time ago, I asked on Stack Exchange <http://stackoverflow.com/questions/10405823/changing-the-symbol-in-the-legend-key-in-ggplot2> if it was possible to change the symbol to, say, an upper case "N".  Kohske Takahashi provided the answer. The following code worked using version 0.9.1. The legend symbol was an upper case "N".

      library(ggplot2)
      library(grid)
      df <- expand.grid(x = factor(seq(1:5)), y = factor(seq(1:5)))
      df$Count = seq(1:25)

      ggplot(data = df, aes( x = x, y = y, label = Count, size = Count)) +
          geom_text() +
          scale_size(range = c(2, 10))

      grid.gedit("^key-[-0-9]+$", label = "N")

However, using version 0.9.2, the last line generates an error:
      Error in editDLfromGPath(gPath, specs, strict, grep, global, redraw) :  'gPath' (^key-[-0-9]+$) not found
and the symbol remains a lower case "a".

Is there a way to change the symbol in the legend key in version 0.9.2?

messages.body_plain:
It's definitely not possible anymore to do what the theme_title()
function does, which is to return a function that returns a text grob.

In the old theme system, a theme was a list of functions that returned
grobs. In the new theme system, a themes is a list of lists of
properties.

I haven't tried it, but I think you'd have to run splitString() on the
original title text, and then use that returned text as the title. For
example:

title <- "Marker1 :  Similar to AAA80501.1 Lycopersicon esculentum;
unknown; Solanum lycopersicum unknown oxidase-like protein mRNA,
complete cds; similar to hyoscyamine 6beta-hydroxylase: SwissProt
Accession Number P24397, flavavone-3-hydroxylase: PIR Accession Number
S36233, and ethylene forming enzyme: encoded by GenBank Accession
number M90294 ;cl209ct403cn544 ;COMPLETE ;RESISTANCE(6), FLOWER(71),
FRUIT(7)"

newtitle <- splitString(title, unit(10, "cm"))

qplot(1:10, 1:10) + ggtitle(newtitle)

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: Independent control over axis lines in 0.9.2
messages.subject_clean: Independent control over axis lines in 0.9.2
messages.body_plain:
This is one area where the theme inheritance combined with the default
theme isn't an improvement on the old system...

The problem is that in the default theme_grey(), axis.line is set to
element_blank(), and the two elements that inherit from axis.line,
axis.line.x and axis.line.y, inherit the blank element. Perhaps it
would be a little easier the default for axis.line was this:
theme(axis.line = element_line(colour=NA))

At any rate, this should do the trick - you just need to set axis.line
to something that's not element_blank():

qplot(1:3, 1:3) +
  theme(axis.line = element_line(),

        axis.line.x = element_line(colour = "red", size = 1),
        axis.line.y = element_line(colour = "blue", size = 1))

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: Adapting to new release
messages.body_plain:
There's a discussion on the development list about how to access elements within the grob table. Apparently 0.92 breaks the ability to call it by name.

Dennis Murphy is working on a transition guide for the new themeing system in 0.92, but in the meantime some of the devs should be able to help.

Below is a copy of that email, which might help you with your problem. Sadly, I have no experience with messing with Grobs.

B

Hi everyone -

A couple questions on the main ggplot2 mailing list have gotten me
thinking about how to access grobs in gtable objects. I'm looking for
some feedback about how to go about doing this.

As you may know, ggplot now generates a gtable object. Here's an
example of how to access and view a gtable:

library(ggplot2)
library(grid)

p <- qplot(1:3, 1:3, colour=c("a", "b", "c"))

# Generate the gtable grob
g <- ggplotGrob(p)

# display it
grid.newpage()
grid.draw(g)

# Print gtable
g
# TableGrob (6 x 6) "layout": 9 grobs
#   (1-6,1-6) background: rect[plot.background.rect.489]
#   (4-4,3-3) spacer: absoluteGrob[GRID.absoluteGrob.462]
#   (3-3,4-4) panel: zeroGrob[NULL]
#   (3-3,3-3) axis-l: gTree[GRID.gTree.450]
#   (4-4,4-4) axis-b: absoluteGrob[GRID.absoluteGrob.456]
#   (5-5,4-4) xlab: text[axis.title.x.text.464]
#   (3-3,2-2) ylab: text[axis.title.y.text.466]
#   (3-3,5-5) guide-box: gtable[guide-box]
#   (2-2,4-4) title: text[plot.title.text.487]

# Layout information is stored in the data frame 'layout'
g$layout
#   t l b r z clip       name
# 9 1 1 6 6 0   on background
# 1 3 3 3 3 3  off     axis-l
# 2 4 3 4 3 1  off     spacer
# 3 3 4 3 4 2   on      panel
# 4 4 4 4 4 4  off     axis-b
# 5 5 4 5 4 5  off       xlab
# 6 3 2 3 2 6  off       ylab
# 7 3 5 3 5 7  off  guide-box
# 8 2 4 2 4 8  off      title

# Access a single grob -- this will get the first one listed in the table
g$grobs[[1]]
# rect[plot.background.rect.489]

As you can see, when you print the gtable object, it displays the name
(taken from the 'layout' column in the data frame) followed by the
type of grob, and finally the grob name (in square brackets). For
example, the first entry in the table is named in the gtable layout
"background", but the name of the grob is "plot.background.rec.489".
I'll call these the layoutName and grobName, respectively. The
layoutName is something used by gtable; the grobName is a property of
the grob itself.

Previously the grobs had grobNames like "background", "axis-l", and so
on. These are now used as the layoutNames, and the grobNames generally
aren't nice and simple like this.

Here are a couple things that seem to be more difficult now:
- I don't think there's a simple way of accessing the grobs by name.
- grid.ls <http://grid.ls/>() no longer produces a nice tree of the grob hierarchy.

Any thoughts on how these things could be improved, and what else
could be improved? There may be some other things I'm missing -- feel
free to chime in.

messages.subject: Re: Adapting to new release
messages.body_plain:
Retrieving it from the ggplot grob is much more complicated now, because of the lack of easy accessor functions in the new gtable structure used by ggplot. It's possible, but ugly. The hard thing about getting the scale breaks is that they're not computed until the ggplot object is rendered, which probably why you had to extract it from the grob in the past.

You can get similar information is to create a scale and train it on your data. For example, this will create a continuous x scale object, train it on the values 1:10, and then retrieve information about the breaks, labels, and range.

sc <- scale_x_continuous()
scale_train_df(sc, data.frame(x = 1:10))
ggplot2:::scale_break_info(sc)

This can be done without even creating a ggplot object. The drawback is that if your plot has stats that modify the data, then the breaks won't match what you get here.

If you must get the labels from the grob, here's some code that does that. Like I said before, it's ugly:
# Create a grob from ggplot
p <- qplot(1:3, 1:3, colour=1:3)
g <- ggplotGrob(p)

# Print the layout.

g$layout
#   t l b r z clip       name
# 9 1 1 6 6 0   on background
# 1 3 3 3 3 3  off     axis-l
# 2 4 3 4 3 1  off     spacer
# 3 3 4 3 4 2   on      panel
# 4 4 4 4 4 4  off     axis-b
# 5 5 4 5 4 5  off       xlab
# 6 3 2 3 2 6  off       ylab
# 7 3 5 3 5 7  off  guide-box
# 8 2 4 2 4 8  off      title

# Here's a simple accessor functions for the grobs:
gt_getgrob <- function(gt, pattern) {
  idx <- grep(pattern, gt$layout$name)
  if (length(idx) > 1)
    stop("More than one match for pattern '", pattern, "'")

  gt$grobs[[idx]]
}

# Get each of the axes
axis_l <- gt_getgrob(g, "axis-l")
axis_b <- gt_getgrob(g, "axis-b")

# Draw them
grid.newpage()
grid.draw(axis_l)
grid.draw(axis_b)

# Extract the labels
axis_l$children[[2]]$grobs[[1]]$label
axis_r$children[[2]]$grobs[[2]]$label

-Winston

I do not believe that throwing away random data should be considered a
desirable feature.

If you are dealing with over-lapping points then you should try assigning an
alpha-level to either the geom itself or the color (alpha("blue", .10))

Otherwise you should probably consider alternative forms of visualization.
Binning with a tile-map would be worth considering.

A lot depends on the actual data...

messages.subject: Re: Defining theme in v0.9.2 -- Error: Don't know how to add o to a plot
messages.subject_clean: Defining theme in v0.9.2 -- Error: Don't know how to add o to a plot
messages.body_plain:
The underlying data structures have changed, so that code won't work
anymore. You can use theme_bw as an example:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/blob/ggplot2-0.9.2/R/theme-defaults.r

theme_bw <- function(base_size = 12, base_family = "") {
  # Starts with theme_grey and then modify some parts
  theme_grey(base_size = base_size, base_family = base_family) %+replace%
    theme(
      axis.text         = element_text(size = rel(0.8)),
      axis.ticks        = element_line(colour = "black"),
      legend.key        = element_rect(colour = "grey80"),
      panel.background  = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      panel.border      = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = "grey50"),
      panel.grid.major  = element_line(colour = "grey90", size = 0.2),
      panel.grid.minor  = element_line(colour = "grey98", size = 0.5),
      strip.background  = element_rect(fill = "grey80", colour = "grey50"),
      strip.background  = element_rect(fill = "grey80", colour = "grey50")
    )
}

There's also a document that describes the changes:
https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/wiki/New-theme-system

-Winston

messages.subject: Supeimposing Plot on Raster Image
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,
I am used to producing R plots with different packages (though I rely
most of the time on ggplot2).
For some presentation, it would be nice to overlay one R-generated
plot on a custom picture (a jpeg or png file most of the time) which
is NOT generated via an R script.
I wonder if this can be done from inside R i.e. if I can generate a
plot e.g. with ggplot2 and then read and use as a background to the
plot an image file.
I found some online discussion about this

http://finzi.psych.upenn.edu/R/Rhelp02a/archive/66704.html
http://journal.r-project.org/archive/2011-1/RJournal_2011-1_Murrell.pdf
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/10318868/how-to-overlay-level-plots-in-r

but none of them involves ggplot2.
I found something about geographical maps and ggplot2, but I need
something flexible enough to superimpose a ggplot2 plot on a
non-vectorial image.
Any suggestion (and above all minimal example) would help me a lot.
Cheers

Lorenzo

I thought I'd pass this along to the list... In another email, Hadley pointed out a better way to get the break information:

p <- qplot(1:3, 1:3, colour=c("a", "b", "c"))

print(p)$panel$ranges

-Winston

On Sat, Sep 8, 2012 at 12:13 AM, Winston Chang <winsto...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Retrieving it from the ggplot grob is much more complicated now, because of the lack of easy accessor functions in the new gtable structure used by ggplot. It's possible, but ugly. The hard thing about getting the scale breaks is that they're not computed until the ggplot object is rendered, which probably why you had to extract it from the grob in the past.
>
> You can get similar information is to create a scale and train it on your data. For example, this will create a continuous x scale object, train it on the values 1:10, and then retrieve information about the breaks, labels, and range.
>
> sc <- scale_x_continuous()
> scale_train_df(sc, data.frame(x = 1:10))
> ggplot2:::scale_break_info(sc)
>
> This can be done without even creating a ggplot object. The drawback is that if your plot has stats that modify the data, then the breaks won't match what you get here.
>
>
>
> If you must get the labels from the grob, here's some code that does that. Like I said before, it's ugly:
> # Create a grob from ggplot
> p <- qplot(1:3, 1:3, colour=1:3)
> g <- ggplotGrob(p)
>
> # Print the layout.
> g$layout
> #   t l b r z clip       name
> # 9 1 1 6 6 0   on background
> # 1 3 3 3 3 3  off     axis-l
> # 2 4 3 4 3 1  off     spacer
> # 3 3 4 3 4 2   on      panel
> # 4 4 4 4 4 4  off     axis-b
> # 5 5 4 5 4 5  off       xlab
> # 6 3 2 3 2 6  off       ylab
> # 7 3 5 3 5 7  off  guide-box
> # 8 2 4 2 4 8  off      title
>
> # Here's a simple accessor functions for the grobs:
> gt_getgrob <- function(gt, pattern) {
>   idx <- grep(pattern, gt$layout$name)
>   if (length(idx) > 1)
>     stop("More than one match for pattern '", pattern, "'")
>
>   gt$grobs[[idx]]
> }
>
>
> # Get each of the axes
> axis_l <- gt_getgrob(g, "axis-l")
> axis_b <- gt_getgrob(g, "axis-b")
>
> # Draw them
> grid.newpage()
> grid.draw(axis_l)
> grid.draw(axis_b)
>
>
> # Extract the labels
> axis_l$children[[2]]$grobs[[1]]$label
> axis_r$children[[2]]$grobs[[2]]$label
>
>
> -Winston
>
>
>
> On Friday, September 7, 2012, Dianne Cook wrote:
> > I used these functions to get the text for the tick marks of an axis in the previous version of ggplot2. It now throws an error about gTree. Anybody know what the best way to get the axis tick labels with the new version??

On 2012-Sep-11, at 00:06 , Lorenzo Isella <lorenzo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I end up with an array m whose dimensions are (x,y,3), hence the script crashes because m[,,4] cannot be addressed.

No alpha channel in your PNG? dimensions 1, 2 and 3 are probably R, G, B and dimension 4 would be the alpha (transparency) channel. Just put a fixed value in there:

w <- matrix(rgb(m[,,1], m[,,2], m[,,3], 0.2), nrow=dim(m)[1])

or

w <- matrix(rgb(m[,,1], m[,,2], m[,,3], rep(0.2, times=length(m[,,3])), nrow=dim(m)[1])

if the code needs vectors of the same length.

The most straightforward way is to make x in data be a factor with all
the possible levels (1 through 6). Then you just need a
scale_fill_discrete call to include all levels.

data = data.frame(x=factor(c(1,2,3,2,2), levels=1:6))
ggplot(data,aes(x=1,fill=x)) +
   geom_bar(position="stack") +
   scale_fill_discrete(drop=FALSE)

Hello,
First of all thanks to you and Roman for helping me out with this.
I think I have finally sorted out the situation.
Please find below at the end of the email a short snippet which does what
I need (at least for the case of a png file without alpha channel).
Cheers

Lorenzo

#####################################################

library(png)
library(gridExtra)
library(grid)
library(ggplot2)

messages.subject: ordering with respect to stacking
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Had a question about stacking if anyone has time.

Not sure if it's unique to factors with three levels, but was having difficulty arranging stacks in a bar plot in the order required.

The following example shows that changing the orders of the factor impacts the color pattern, but not the position of the levels in the stack. On the other hand, using the diamonds dataset, I was able to make the desired adjustment, so it's unclear to me what's unique about my example.

Here's the example showing how changing the order of factors changes the colours assigned to each level, but doesn't impact the position of levels in the stack (as desired and which is achievable with the diamonds dataset).

        tst<-data.frame(y=c(1,1,1,2,2,2,3,3,3),x=c("a","a","a","b","b","b","c","c","c"),z=rep(c("x","y","z"),3))

        tst$z2<-factor(tst$z,levels=c("z","y","x"))

        ggplot(tst,aes(x,y))+geom_bar(stat="identity",aes(fill=z2),position="stack")
        ggplot(tst,aes(x,y))+geom_bar(stat="identity",aes(fill=z),position="stack")

Thanks very much for the help! Once again.

Adam Loveland

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I figured out that my problem was caused by how ggplot handles holes in polygons, as Winston mentioned. I wasn't aware that ggplot plots holes as a separate polygon above the land polygon (in this case) and not as a true hole, I can get the caspian sea to show up if I set "fill = hole". However, It's not an ideal solutions as I want all water area to be transparent.

Thanks!
Kristoffer

messages.subject: Is it possible to extract color information and values from scale_color_gradientn()?
messages.subject_clean: Is it possible to extract color information and values from scale_color_gradientn()?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm interested in extracting the color values that's used in scale_color_gradientn(), for instance take this example code:

library(ggplot2)

z <- rgamma(1000, shape=0.2, scale=10000)
hist(z)
x <- data.frame("x" = runif(1000), y=runif(1000), z=z)

my_cols <- c("#fef29f", "#fee47c", "#fed158", "#feb934", "#fe8b29", "#fe581e", "#ef2c19", "#df1424", "#cb0f39", "#b60b4b", "#a10757", "#8d045f", "#780262", "#640060")
my_vals <- c(0.1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000, 2500, 5000, 10000, 25000, 50000)

ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, fill=z, color=z), data = x) +
  geom_point(size=3) +
  scale_color_gradientn(colours=my_cols, values=my_vals, na.value="#f9fff1", rescaler = function(x, ...) x, oob = identity)

Here, I'm interested in extracting color values for each value in z. Basically I want to create a color legend for all values in z. I is possible to extract this from ggplot?

Thanks!

/Kristoffer Magnusson

messages.subject: Re: geom_points data capacity?
messages.body_plain:
Hoi,

The following

require(ggplot2)
zz <- data.frame( xx <- runif(n=750000 ), yy <- runif(n=750000) )
ggplot(zz,aes(x=xx,y=yy))+geom_point()

takes about a minute to plot on my machine  ( dual core, 4Gig )

But with so many point you might want to use a different kind of plot,
or just plot a sample of data.

If you save such a plot as pdf it will take a very long time to render too.

Frans.

library(ggplot2)

        geom_errorbar( aes(ymax = est+se,  ymin = est),  width=.25, position =dodge)+
        scale_fill_manual(values=c("#996633","black"))+
       xlab("")+
       ylab("Percentage - Current Smokers")   +
       labs (spd=" ")+

messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

Thanks Jonas for your reply.

The solution for this problem is to remove the attribute "width = 0.5" in line 5. The bars will dodge at width =1 specified in line 2. The value 0.25 for width of error bars will be applied as in line 6. Make sure you don't double quote the attribute dodge throughout your code, otherwise it will assume the default dodge value that is 0.9.

This problem may have to do something with inheritance while creating instances of an object.

The upshot is run your code as it is and after deleting width=0.5 in line 5. In other words, line 5 should be ...geom_bar(position=dodge)... but not ...geom_bar(position=dodge, width=0.50)... If you want to tweak the width of bar dodging and error bars, you have adjust the value of width in line 2 for bar dodging and adjust the value of width in line 6 for error bar.

Sathish

Hi,
In my previous message, I explained adjusting the value of width in line 2 would alter the width of "bar dodging". But, it would not assist in controlling the width of the "bar" itself.  The solution from Jonas gives a fine control over the width of the bar and the error bar.

Here is the modified code:

library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(data = tempdata,
            aes(x = age, y = est, fill = spd)) +

              geom_bar(position="dodge", width=0.50) +

              geom_errorbar( aes(ymax = est+se,  ymin = est),

                             position = position_dodge(width=0.5), width=0.25)+
                               ...
To tweak the width of the bar, adjust the value in line 4. Notice the double quote in geom_bar(position="dodge", width...) in line 4. If you remove double quote, you will see overlapping of dodged bars which is not what I expect in my bar chart. Probably someone can explain the significance of double quotes specifically to this problem and in general for all ggplot2 graphs.

For error bar, there are two values specified in line 6. One is for the placing the error bar at a position having half of the specified value in position_dodge(width=0.5), so this value can be same as the value in line 4 in order for the error bar be placed at the center, and the second value is for adjusting the width of the error bar: width = 0.25.

Sathish

Hi:

On Mon, Sep 17, 2012 at 11:19 AM, pradip...@samhsa.hhs.gov <pradip...@samhsa.hhs.gov> wrote:

Harmless warning.

>

>
> 2)  I don't get the desired results for: axis.title.y = theme_text(size = 10, face = "bold".  In the output of the chart, the title of the y-axis is of the small fonti size and not emboldedened.

In theory, the code seems OK on the surface, but I wonder if ggplot2 adjusted on the fly because the y-axis margin was being pushed, possibly by the font size of the axis labels. (If so, see the theme element plot.margin.)

Additional comments:

1. You have two typos in the code: vsust should be vjust and cigarette rather than cigatette.
2. In the latest version of ggplot2 (0.9.2), the new theming system allows you to better organize common argument values. Here's what I *think* it would look like under the new system:

ggplot(...) + ... +
    theme(text = element_text(size = 25, face = "bold"),  # default text size and type face
              axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0),
              axis.text.y = element_text(hjust = 1),
              axis.title = element_text(size = rel(0.4)),
              axis.title.x = element_text( face = "plain"),
              legend.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8), hjust = 0),
              legend.position = "bottom")

This specification illustrates several of the features of the new theming system:
   * theme()  replaces opts()
   * element_xx()  replaces  theme_xx()
   * text is now a (top level) theme element along with line and rect;
     the other two new theme elements are axis.text and strip.text
   * the new theming system supports inheritance of theme properties =>
     theme elements now have a hierarchical structure
   * the new system supports relative sizing (e.g., rel(0.4)) -
     this is advantageous if you change the base size but want to maintain
     proportionality of sizes of related theme elements.

This is why I specified size = 25 (it makes the later relative sizes easier to define) in the top level theme element text - all other text-related theme elements inherit that as the base size unless you specify otherwise with element_text(). Similarly, axis.title.x and axis.title.y inherit from axis.title (similarly for axis.text). The idea is to streamline the amount of code written and to be more computationally efficient in handling these aspects of a ggplot.

Caveat emptor on these suggestions since you did not supply a reproducible example.

Dennis

In theory, the code seems OK on the surface, but I wonder if ggplot2 adjusted on the fly because the y-axis margin was being pushed, possibly by the font size of the axis labels. (If so, see the theme element plot.margin.)

Additional comments:

1. You have two typos in the code: vsust should be vjust and cigarette rather than cigatette.
2. In the latest version of ggplot2 (0.9.2), the new theming system allows you to better organize common argument values. Here's what I *think* it would look like under the new system:

ggplot(...) + ... +
    theme(text = element_text(size = 25, face = "bold"),  # default text size and type face
              axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0),
              axis.text.y = element_text(hjust = 1),
              axis.title = element_text(size = rel(0.4)),
              axis.title.x = element_text( face = "plain"),
              legend.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8), hjust = 0),
              legend.position = "bottom")

This specification illustrates several of the features of the new theming system:
   * theme()  replaces opts()
   * element_xx()  replaces  theme_xx()
   * text is now a (top level) theme element along with line and rect;
     the other two new theme elements are axis.text and strip.text
   * the new theming system supports inheritance of theme properties =>
     theme elements now have a hierarchical structure
   * the new system supports relative sizing (e.g., rel(0.4)) -
     this is advantageous if you change the base size but want to maintain
     proportionality of sizes of related theme elements.

This is why I specified size = 25 (it makes the later relative sizes easier to define) in the top level theme element text - all other text-related theme elements inherit that as the base size unless you specify otherwise with element_text(). Similarly, axis.title.x and axis.title.y inherit from axis.title (similarly for axis.text). The idea is to streamline the amount of code written and to be more computationally efficient in handling these aspects of a ggplot.

Caveat emptor on these suggestions since you did not supply a reproducible example.

Dennis

Thanks,

messages.subject: Re: Reference line in all plots of facet wrap
messages.subject_clean: Reference line in all plots of facet wrap
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

The function ggplot_build() is one way to grab information like this from a plot, but in the future, this will probably be controlled by the gtable package if it is not already. The group mapping was unnecessary so I removed it.

p <- qplot(temperature, DN, color=Image, data=vthcal1MIDAScal1m,
          geom=c("point","smooth"), method="lm") +
     facet_wrap(~Image,ncol=2)

line_data <- ggplot_build(p)$data[[2]]
line_data <- subset(line_data, PANEL == 1)
p + geom_line(data = line_data, aes(x = x, y = y, color = colour))

Another way to have gone about this would have been to fit linear models to each subset of data first, extracted their intercepts and slopes, and then used geom_abline(). For the reference line, I just plugged in the values of intercept and slope.

lmcoef <- ddply(vthcal1MIDAScal1m, "Image",
                   function(d) coef(lm(DN ~ temperature, data = d)))
names(lmcoef) <- c("Image", "b0", "b1")

ggplot(data=vthcal1MIDAScal1m, aes(x = temperature, y = DN)) +
    geom_point(aes(color = Image)) +
    geom_abline(data = lmcoef, aes(intercept = b0, slope = b1, color = Image)) +
    geom_abline(intercept = 29468.87, slope = 124.6561, color = "red") +
    facet_wrap(~ Image, ncol = 2)

I used ggplot() in this case because you want color to be mapped to points and the first call to geom_abline(), but not the second.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
I think you should be getting the following warning: “ymax not defined: adjusting position using y instead”.

To understand more about this warning, refer this ggplot2 group discussion specifically to Hadley’s comment at the bottom of this page: https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!topic/ggplot2/PGzx4u6U84Y

I would suggest you to remove ylim (0,55) + and instead, aesthetically map the ymin to 0 and ymax to 60 (as Dennis suggested) in line 1. See the modified code. Let me know if your still getting this warning.

tempdata <- read.table("d1.txt", header = TRUE, sep = " ")

dim(tempdata)

tempdata$spd <- factor(tempdata$spd,

                       levels=c ("No","Yes"),

                       labels=c('No SPD', 'SPD'),

                       ordered=TRUE)

tempdata$age <- factor (tempdata$age,

                        levels=c ('75+', '65-74', '45-64', '18-44'),

                        ordered=TRUE)

library("ggplot2")

loadedNamespaces()

#[1] "base"         "colorspace"   "datasets"     "dichromat"    "digest"       "ggplot2"      "graphics"     "grDevices"

# [9] "grid"         "gtable"       "labeling"     "MASS"         "memoise"      "methods"      "munsell"      "plyr"

#[17] "proto"        "RColorBrewer" "reshape2"     "scales"       "stats"        "stringr"      "tools"        "utils"

p <- ggplot(data = tempdata, aes(x = age, y = est, ymin=0, ymax=60, fill = spd)) +

         geom_bar(position="dodge", stat="identity", width=0.50) +

        geom_text (aes(label=round(est,1)), position=position_dodge(width=0.9),

                hjust=-.1, vjust=-.1, colour="red", size=8) +

        scale_fill_manual(values=c("black", "#996633"))+

        labs (x = "  ", y= "Current Cigarette Use (%)",  fill=" ")+

        coord_flip()+

          theme(text = element_text(size = 25, face = "bold"),

              axis.text.x = element_text(vjust = 0, colour="black"),

              axis.text.y = element_text(hjust = 1, colour="black"),

              axis.title.y = element_text(size = rel(0.4), colour="black"),

              axis.title.x = element_text( face = "plain"),

              legend.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8), hjust = 0),

              legend.position = "bottom")

print (p)

ggsave(file='test_curr_smk_spd.png', width=11, height=7)

HTH

Sathish

Hi,

I would appreciate if someone could advise me on resolving the following two issues:

1)  Although I got the bar chart correct, I could not figure out why I got the following message after each of the last two lines of the code in the console: ymax not defined: adjusting position using y instead

Harmless warning.

2)  I don't get the desired results for: axis.title.y = theme_text(size = 10, face = "bold".  In the output of the chart, the title of the y-axis is of the small fonti size and not emboldedened.

In theory, the code seems OK on the surface, but I wonder if ggplot2 adjusted on the fly because the y-axis margin was being pushed, possibly by the font size of the axis labels. (If so, see the theme element plot.margin.)

Additional comments:

1. You have two typos in the code: vsust should be vjust and cigarette rather than cigatette.
2. In the latest version of ggplot2 (0.9.2), the new theming system allows you to better organize common argument values. Here's what I *think* it would look like under the new system:

ggplot(...) + ... +
    theme(text = element_text(size = 25, face = "bold"),  # default text size and type face
              axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0),
              axis.text.y = element_text(hjust = 1),
              axis.title = element_text(size = rel(0.4)),
              axis.title.x = element_text( face = "plain"),
              legend.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8), hjust = 0),
              legend.position = "bottom")

This specification illustrates several of the features of the new theming system:
   * theme()  replaces opts()
   * element_xx()  replaces  theme_xx()
   * text is now a (top level) theme element along with line and rect;
     the other two new theme elements are axis.text and strip.text
   * the new theming system supports inheritance of theme properties =>
     theme elements now have a hierarchical structure
   * the new system supports relative sizing (e.g., rel(0.4)) -
     this is advantageous if you change the base size but want to maintain
     proportionality of sizes of related theme elements.

This is why I specified size = 25 (it makes the later relative sizes easier to define) in the top level theme element text - all other text-related theme elements inherit that as the base size unless you specify otherwise with element_text(). Similarly, axis.title.x and axis.title.y inherit from axis.title (similarly for axis.text). The idea is to streamline the amount of code written and to be more computationally efficient in handling these aspects of a ggplot.

Caveat emptor on these suggestions since you did not supply a reproducible example.

Dennis

Thanks,

Pradip Muhuri

library('ggplot2')

   scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar)

                       levels=c ("No","Yes"),

                        levels=c ('75+', '65-74', '45-64', '18-44'),

Hi,

I would appreciate if someone could advise me on resolving the following two issues:

1)  Although I got the bar chart correct, I could not figure out why I got the following message after each of the last two lines of the code in the console: ymax not defined: adjusting position using y instead

Harmless warning.

2)  I don't get the desired results for: axis.title.y = theme_text(size = 10, face = "bold".  In the output of the chart, the title of the y-axis is of the small fonti size and not emboldedened.

In theory, the code seems OK on the surface, but I wonder if ggplot2 adjusted on the fly because the y-axis margin was being pushed, possibly by the font size of the axis labels. (If so, see the theme element plot.margin.)

Additional comments:

1. You have two typos in the code: vsust should be vjust and cigarette rather than cigatette.
2. In the latest version of ggplot2 (0.9.2), the new theming system allows you to better organize common argument values. Here's what I *think* it would look like under the new system:

ggplot(...) + ... +
    theme(text = element_text(size = 25, face = "bold"),  # default text size and type face
              axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0),
              axis.text.y = element_text(hjust = 1),
              axis.title = element_text(size = rel(0.4)),
              axis.title.x = element_text( face = "plain"),
              legend.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8), hjust = 0),
              legend.position = "bottom")

This specification illustrates several of the features of the new theming system:
   * theme()  replaces opts()
   * element_xx()  replaces  theme_xx()
   * text is now a (top level) theme element along with line and rect;
     the other two new theme elements are axis.text and strip.text
   * the new theming system supports inheritance of theme properties =>
     theme elements now have a hierarchical structure
   * the new system supports relative sizing (e.g., rel(0.4)) -
     this is advantageous if you change the base size but want to maintain
     proportionality of sizes of related theme elements.

This is why I specified size = 25 (it makes the later relative sizes easier to define) in the top level theme element text - all other text-related theme elements inherit that as the base size unless you specify otherwise with element_text(). Similarly, axis.title.x and axis.title.y inherit from axis.title (similarly for axis.text). The idea is to streamline the amount of code written and to be more computationally efficient in handling these aspects of a ggplot.

Caveat emptor on these suggestions since you did not supply a reproducible example.

Dennis

Thanks,

Pradip Muhuri

messages.subject: geom_pointrange and limits on scale_y_continuous
messages.body_plain:
I recently plotted some data using geom_pointrange and was surprised at how that geom behaved when I set limits on the scale.  This code should illustrate things:

d<-data.frame(x=c(1,2),y=c(0.01,0))
p<-ggplot(d)+geom_pointrange(aes(x=x,y=y,ymin=y-0.1,ymax=y+0.1))+scale_y_continuous(limits=c(-0.095,0.11))
print(p)

The limits on the scale are such that they clip the ymin of the second data point.  I had figured I would end up with an error bar extending to the lower edge of the plot.  Failing that, I figured the geom for that data point would be removed entirely from the plot.  What I got was surprisingly in between those two extremes.  The error bar was gone but the central value was plotted.  In my case, this led to several minutes of confusion as I tried to figure out what was going on.

I think the appearance of a geom should be "atomic"; it's either there or it isn't.  For points, this is natural, but for extended geoms, I guess one could debate what the behavior ought to be. Should you show the portion of the geom within the range of the plot (in other words, have a behavior like you'd get with coord_cartesian) or should the geom be gone entirely?  Plotting part of the geom (in this case, just the central value) seems like the wrong thing to do.

I would suggest you to remove ylim (0,55) + and instead, aesthetically map the ymin to 0 and ymax to 60 (as Dennis suggested) in line 1. See the modified code. Let me know if your still getting this warning.

dim(tempdata)

tempdata$spd <- factor(tempdata$spd,

                       levels=c ("No","Yes"),

                       labels=c('No SPD', 'SPD'),

                       ordered=TRUE)

                        levels=c ('75+', '65-74', '45-64', '18-44'),

library("ggplot2")

loadedNamespaces()

#[1] "base"         "colorspace"   "datasets"     "dichromat"    "digest"       "ggplot2"      "graphics"     "grDevices"

p <- ggplot(data = tempdata, aes(x = age, y = est, ymin=0, ymax=60, fill = spd)) +

         geom_bar(position="dodge", stat="identity", width=0.50) +

        geom_text (aes(label=round(est,1)), position=position_dodge(width=0.9),

                hjust=-.1, vjust=-.1, colour="red", size=8) +

        scale_fill_manual(values=c("black", "#996633"))+

        labs (x = "  ", y= "Current Cigarette Use (%)",  fill=" ")+

              axis.text.y = element_text(hjust = 1, colour="black"),

              axis.title.y = element_text(size = rel(0.4), colour="black"),

              axis.title.x = element_text( face = "plain"),

print (p)

ggsave(file='test_curr_smk_spd.png', width=11, height=7)

I would appreciate if someone could advise me on resolving the following two issues:

1)  Although I got the bar chart correct, I could not figure out why I got the following message after each of the last two lines of the code in the console: ymax not defined: adjusting position using y instead

Harmless warning.

2)  I don't get the desired results for: axis.title.y = theme_text(size = 10, face = "bold".  In the output of the chart, the title of the y-axis is of the small fonti size and not emboldedened.

In theory, the code seems OK on the surface, but I wonder if ggplot2 adjusted on the fly because the y-axis margin was being pushed, possibly by the font size of the axis labels. (If so, see the theme element plot.margin.)

Additional comments:

1. You have two typos in the code: vsust should be vjust and cigarette rather than cigatette.
2. In the latest version of ggplot2 (0.9.2), the new theming system allows you to better organize common argument values. Here's what I *think* it would look like under the new system:

ggplot(...) + ... +
    theme(text = element_text(size = 25, face = "bold"),  # default text size and type face
              axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0),
              axis.text.y = element_text(hjust = 1),
              axis.title = element_text(size = rel(0.4)),
              axis.title.x = element_text( face = "plain"),
              legend.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8), hjust = 0),
              legend.position = "bottom")

This specification illustrates several of the features of the new theming system:
   * theme()  replaces opts()
   * element_xx()  replaces  theme_xx()
   * text is now a (top level) theme element along with line and rect;
     the other two new theme elements are axis.text and strip.text
   * the new theming system supports inheritance of theme properties =>
     theme elements now have a hierarchical structure
   * the new system supports relative sizing (e.g., rel(0.4)) -
     this is advantageous if you change the base size but want to maintain
     proportionality of sizes of related theme elements.

This is why I specified size = 25 (it makes the later relative sizes easier to define) in the top level theme element text - all other text-related theme elements inherit that as the base size unless you specify otherwise with element_text(). Similarly, axis.title.x and axis.title.y inherit from axis.title (similarly for axis.text). The idea is to streamline the amount of code written and to be more computationally efficient in handling these aspects of a ggplot.

Caveat emptor on these suggestions since you did not supply a reproducible example.

Dennis

Thanks,

Pradip Muhuri

          geom_text (aes(label=round(est,1)), position=position_dodge(width=0.9),

blankground <- function() {
    theme(panel.background = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),

          panel.margin = unit(0,"null"),
          plot.margin = rep(unit(0,"null"),4),

          axis.ticks = element_blank(),
          axis.text.x = element_blank(),
          axis.text.y = element_blank(),
          axis.title.x = element_blank(),
          axis.title.y = element_blank(),

messages.body_plain:
When you call svg() or ggsave(), try adding the option
useDingbats=FALSE. By default, R uses the Dingbats font for point
symbols, and this can sometimes cause problems.

It's also possible that making the Dingbats font available to Inkscape
will solve the issue, but I haven't tested this.

messages.body_plain:

I don't think this has anything to do with round()

[1] 24

[1] "24.0" "24.1"

messages.subject_clean: Manual labels in legend for a continuous size?
messages.body_plain:
Hey,

I suspect this should be trivial, but it's a thorough headache thus far ...

I'm transforming the size of a text geom by the natural logarithm. In the legend, I would like use a custom set of breaks and labels.

data <- data.frame(X=-30:30, Y=sample(1:100, size=61), T=exp(runif(61, 1, 10)),
                   L=sample(letters, size=61, replace=TRUE))
g <- ggplot(data=data, aes(x=X, y=Y, size=T, label=L))
g <- g +  geom_text() + scale_size(trans="log", range=c(.1, 20))
print(g)

How can tweak the legend so that it shows just three entries that are at preset values (20, 150, 1000), for example? I would like to supply nice numbers there and also get rid of the digits behind the decimal point.

Thank you.

messages.subject: Re: Symbol Size in Legend Key
messages.body_plain:
keywidth and keyheight will only changes the size of the grey box surrounding each legend key.
To change the size (or colour or alpha) of the actual legend keys you should use the 'override.aes' option.
e.g.
guides(colour=guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 4)))

Roey

messages.subject: RE: Manual labels in legend for a continuous size?
messages.subject_clean: Manual labels in legend for a continuous size?
messages.body_plain:
Forgot to push “reply all” yesterday. Here is my comment again. If you want to manually change the size without wanting to use log transformation inside scale_size () function, then you can transform the data before you do ggplot. I would better do transformation while creating ggplot.

data <- data.frame(X=-30:30, Y=sample(1:100, size=61), T=exp(runif(61, 1, 10)),

                   L=sample(letters, size=61, replace=TRUE))

data$T <- log(data$T)

g <- ggplot(data=data, aes(x=X, y=Y, size=T, label=L))

g <- g + geom_text() + scale_size(range = c(5, 20))

print(g)

HTH

Sathish

From: Srinivasan, Sathish K
Sent: Thursday, September 20, 2012 5:21 PM
To: 'Tobee'
Subject: RE: Manual labels in legend for a continuous size?

Try something like this

data <- data.frame(X=-30:30, Y=sample(1:100, size=61), T=exp(runif(61, 1, 8)),

                   L=sample(letters, size=61, replace=TRUE))

g <- ggplot(data=data, aes(x=X, y=Y, size=T, label=L))

g <- g + geom_text() + scale_size(trans="log10", range=c(3, 18))

print(g)

The maximum power of e for “T” can be tried with different numbers.

Log transformation can be toggled between 2, 10 or any.

HTH,

-Sathish

From: ggp...@googlegroups.com [mailto:ggp...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of Tobee
Sent: Thursday, September 20, 2012 12:47 PM
To: ggp...@googlegroups.com

Hey,

I suspect this should be trivial, but it's a thorough headache thus far ...

I'm transforming the size of a text geom by the natural logarithm. In the legend, I would like use a custom set of breaks and labels.

data <- data.frame(X=-30:30, Y=sample(1:100, size=61), T=exp(runif(61, 1, 10)),

                   L=sample(letters, size=61, replace=TRUE))

g <- ggplot(data=data, aes(x=X, y=Y, size=T, label=L))

g <- g +  geom_text() + scale_size(trans="log", range=c(.1, 20))

print(g)

How can tweak the legend so that it shows just three entries that are at preset values (20, 150, 1000), for example? I would like to supply nice numbers there and also get rid of the digits behind the decimal point.

Thank you.

messages.subject: Re: new ggts package
messages.body_plain:
There is some demand - for example the tis package has had nberShade.ggplot (adds recessions to ggplot2 graphs) and fortify.tis (create a data frame from tis time series objects) for a couple of years.

You should probably rename as.zoo.df to fortify.zoo since ``fortify`` is the standard function for creating data frames for future plotting with ggplot2.

I also like some kind of autoplot construct like this.

autoplot.zoo <- function(x, ...) {
    if(is.null(ncol(x)) == 1) {
        qplot(as.Date(time(x)), coredata(x), geom="line") + xlab("") + ylab(substitute(x))
    } else if(ncol(x) == 1) {
        qplot(as.Date(time(x)), as.vector(coredata(x)), geom="line") + xlab("") + ylab(substitute(x))
    } else {
        df <- data.frame(time=as.Date(time(x)), coredata(x))
        dfm <- reshape2::melt(df, id.vars="time", variable.name <http://variable.name>="series")
        qplot(time, value, data=dfm, geom="line", group=series, colour=series, linetype=series)
    }
}

viewports. A workaround for now is to use a nonzero size for
axis.ticks.margin, like this:

The bug has been fixed in the development branch of R, so this problem
should go away in R 2.16.

For more info, see:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/636

messages.subject: Re: New documentation online
messages.body_plain:
A few suggestions:

1) Include a link on how to install R or get R.  I say this because I
think that ggplot2 has grown large enough people may find it before
they find R---that is they may see a cool graphic, see that it was
made in ggplot2 and then want to learn more.
2) I think it would be great to have a list of resources for learning
ggplot2 up on the main website.  Off the top of my head, Dennis'
transition guide and the theme guide either as webpages or PDFs would
be good.  What I would really love is something like Hadley's ggplot2
book, but available all online (and updated for the most recent
version of ggplot2).  Perhaps this could be something on github that
the community could help with the maintenance of and then is just
periodically checked and built for the website.

I work at a university statistical consulting center that has
traditionally focused primarily on supporting Stata, SAS, and SPSS.  I
have been putting a lot of work into expanding the resources we have
available for R in person and on our (freely available) website and I
make heavy use of ggplot2 for data exploration and presentation of
model results (e.g., http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/R/dae/ztnb.htm).
However, I do not really have good resources to _introduce_ ggplot2.
If I could say, "There are a couple great guides and introductions to
ggplot2 as well as all the documentation on its website, ggplot2.org <http://ggplot2.org>"
that would be fantastic.  I think a lot of the clients I see are
impressed with the graphs, but feel overwhelmed to do it themselves.
Final products are great for display, but poor for teaching.

I have to say overall I am so impressed with Hadley and this
community.  In addition to his own amazing work, Hadley has managed to
engage and catalyze others to make ggplot2, the website, the
documentation, and the community an exemplar for any software project.
 The graphics and features are par none.

Cheers,

Josh

messages.subject: Re: Question on scales = "free_y""
messages.body_plain:
I think the problem is that scales="free" doesn't work with coord_flip. This is a limitation of ggplot2.

See here:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/673

 If it's very important to have free scales and use the same orientation that you're currently using, I would suggest rewriting it to not use coord_flip, by swapping the x and y variables, changing vline to hline, and replacing the pointrange with a point and a segment.

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: Align four Plots in one graph with same length of y-and x-axis
messages.subject_clean: Align four Plots in one graph with same length of y-and x-axis
messages.body_plain:
Here is a quick example:

library(grid)
library(plyr)
library(gtable)

ps <- dlply(mtcars, .(vs, am), function(d)
ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(ggplot(d, aes(cyl, mpg)) + geom_point())))
r <- rbind(cbind(ps[[1]], ps[[2]], size = "first"), cbind(ps[[3]],
ps[[4]], size = "first"), size = "first")
grid.draw(r)

Winston and Hadley, cbind.gtable and rbind.gtable cannot work with
size = min/max in some cases.

kohske

messages.body_plain:
Building off of Kohske's example, you can pull out the pieces of the original gtable, and put them into another gtable, so you don't have to mess with grid viewports.

library(gtable)
library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(cyl, fill = factor(gear))) + geom_bar() +
    facet_wrap(~am+vs, nrow = 1)
gt <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p))

# We can render gt
grid.newpage()
grid.draw(g)

# Display the layout of gt
gtable_show_layout(gt)

# Create the gtable with one col and two rows
g <- gtable(widths = unit(1, "null"), heights = unit(c(1, 1), "null"))

# Pull out all columns from gt, except the last column, which has the legend
# Put it on the first row of the new gtable
g <- gtable_add_grob(g, gt[, -15], t=1, l=1, b=1, r=1)

# Pull out the legend from gt, and put it in the second row of the new gtable
g <- gtable_add_grob(g, gt[4, 15], t=2, l=1, b=2, r=1)

# Draw the new gtable
grid.newpage()
grid.draw(g)

--Winston

2012/9/19 David Morrison <da...@bnl.gov>:

> I recently plotted some data using geom_pointrange and was surprised at how
> that geom behaved when I set limits on the scale.  This code should
> illustrate things:
>
> d<-data.frame(x=c(1,2),y=c(0.01,0))
> p<-ggplot(d)+geom_pointrange(aes(x=x,y=y,ymin=y-0.1,ymax=y+0.1))+scale_y_continuous(limits=c(-0.095,0.11))
> print(p)
>
> The limits on the scale are such that they clip the ymin of the second data
> point.  I had figured I would end up with an error bar extending to the
> lower edge of the plot.  Failing that, I figured the geom for that data
> point would be removed entirely from the plot.  What I got was surprisingly
> in between those two extremes.  The error bar was gone but the central value
> was plotted.  In my case, this led to several minutes of confusion as I
> tried to figure out what was going on.
>
> I think the appearance of a geom should be "atomic"; it's either there or it
> isn't.  For points, this is natural, but for extended geoms, I guess one
> could debate what the behavior ought to be. Should you show the portion of
> the geom within the range of the plot (in other words, have a behavior like
> you'd get with coord_cartesian) or should the geom be gone entirely?

messages.body_plain:
Here is a 0.9.2 compatible example:

```
p1 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(cyl, mpg, colour = wt)) + geom_point()
p2 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(drat, qsec, colour = wt)) + geom_point()

gt1 <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p1))
gt2 <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p2))

gt <- gtable(widths = unit(c(4, 1), "null"), height = unit(c(1, 1), "null"))
gt <- gtable_add_grob(gt, gt1[, -5], 1, 1)
gt <- gtable_add_grob(gt, gt2[, -5], 2, 1)
gt <- gtable_add_grob(gt, gt1[, 5], 1, 2, 2)

grid.newpage()
grid.draw(gt)
```

messages.subject: Re: geom_pointrange and limits on scale_y_continuous
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, Sep 18, 2012 at 10:46 PM, David Morrison <da...@bnl.gov> wrote:
> I recently plotted some data using geom_pointrange and was surprised at how
> that geom behaved when I set limits on the scale.  This code should
> illustrate things:
>
> d<-data.frame(x=c(1,2),y=c(0.01,0))
> p<-ggplot(d)+geom_pointrange(aes(x=x,y=y,ymin=y-0.1,ymax=y+0.1))+scale_y_continuous(limits=c(-0.095,0.11))
> print(p)
>
> The limits on the scale are such that they clip the ymin of the second data
> point.  I had figured I would end up with an error bar extending to the
> lower edge of the plot.  Failing that, I figured the geom for that data
> point would be removed entirely from the plot.  What I got was surprisingly
> in between those two extremes.  The error bar was gone but the central value
> was plotted.  In my case, this led to several minutes of confusion as I
> tried to figure out what was going on.

The easiest way to understand the behaviour is to think about the data
- all data outside the limits is discarded.

I don't think there's anyway to think about the "atom" of geoms - I
think it would be even more confusing if restricting the limits on a
line removed all points if one was missing.

Hadley

--
RStudio / Rice University

You have to make a data frame to pass to geom_text with that particular facet variables.  Here's an example I stole somewhere to illustrate:

library(ggplot2)
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, wt)) + geom_point()
p <- p + facet_grid(. ~ cyl)
#create a new data frame with the info
ann_text <- data.frame(mpg = 15,wt = 5,lab = "Text",
                       cyl = factor(8,levels = c(4, 6, 8)))
p + geom_text(data = ann_text,label = "Text")

Cheers,
Tyler

I think the problem is that scales="free" doesn't work with coord_flip. This is a limitation of ggplot2.

See here:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/673

 If it's very important to have free scales and use the same orientation that you're currently using, I would suggest rewriting it to not use coord_flip, by swapping the x and y variables, changing vline to hline, and replacing the pointrange with a point and a segment.

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: geom_pointrange and limits on scale_y_continuous
messages.body_plain:
I don't know.  Would it be confusing if the entire line disappeared if one point fell outside the limits of the scale?  Maybe, maybe not, but it also seems to be a moot point, as that is exactly what does happen:

 d<-data.frame(x=c(1,2,3),y=c(1,-1,1))
 p<-ggplot(d)+geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y))+scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,2))
 print(p)

 But let me try a different example:

 d<-data.frame(x=c(1,2),y=c(0,0))
 p<-ggplot(d)+geom_errorbar(aes(x=x,y=y,ymin=y-0.1,ymax=y+0.1))+scale_x_continuous(limits=c(0.5,2.25))
 print(p)

Now the crossbar at each end of the error bar completely disappears because one end of it falls just beyond the scale limit.  I'm not sure how I understand this behavior by focusing on the data.  Do you consider the crossbars to be data?

I guess my point is that there is already some concept of atomicity implicit in the way ggplot2 draws geoms, it's just not consistent.  A point is either there or it's not.  Same for a line.  Not so for pointranges and errorbars, maybe others.  I think consistency in this regard would be a *good* thing, right?

Dave

On Thursday, September 27, 2012 3:26:46 AM UTC-4, Hadley Wickham wrote:

> The easiest way to understand the behaviour is to think about the data
> - all data outside the limits is discarded.
>
> I don't think there's anyway to think about the "atom" of geoms - I
> think it would be even more confusing if restricting the limits on a
> line removed all points if one was missing.

messages.subject: Re: geom_pointrange and limits on scale_y_continuous
messages.body_plain:
I guess I'm destined to lose this argument, but let me gamely take one last crack at it! OK, even though nothing in my data set specified anything about the length of the endcaps on my errorbars, and I because of that I think of them as decoration, I should instead think of them as data and I shouldn't be surprised that they disappear entirely when they stretch beyond the limit specified in my scale.  OK–deep breath–I've internalized that. Got it. Now I'm going to plot some data with big round symbols, the size of which is explicitly controlled by my data set.  Should I expect a plotted point that stretches beyond my scale limits to disappear or not?

 d<-data.frame(x=c(1,3),y=c(1,1),z=c(10,100))
 p<-ggplot(d)+geom_point(aes(x=x,y=y),pch=21,size=d$z)+scale_x_continuous(limits=c(0,3))
 print(p)

(Just so there's no suspense, the second point does not disappear, the portion of the circle within the limits of the scale is drawn.)

On Friday, September 28, 2012 12:24:51 AM UTC-4, Hadley Wickham wrote:
> > I don't know.  Would it be confusing if the entire line disappeared if one
> > point fell outside the limits of the scale?  Maybe, maybe not, but it also
> > seems to be a moot point, as that is exactly what does happen:

> >  d<-data.frame(x=c(1,2,3),y=c(1,-1,1))
> >  p<-ggplot(d)+geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y))+scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,2))
> >  print(p)
>
> Unfortunately you picked an example with only three points, and the
> missing point was in the middle.
>
>  d <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = c(1:5, 5:1))

>
>
> >  But let me try a different example:

> > p<-ggplot(d)+geom_errorbar(aes(x=x,y=y,ymin=y-0.1,ymax=y+0.1))+scale_x_continuous(limits=c(0.5,2.25))
> >  print(p)
> >
> > Now the crossbar at each end of the error bar completely disappears because
> > one end of it falls just beyond the scale limit.  I'm not sure how I

library(ggplot2); library(grid)
d <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(carat, price, fill = ..density..))
    xlim(0, 2) + stat_binhex(na.rm = TRUE) + opts(aspect.ratio = 1)

grob <- ggplotGrob(d)

grob <- editGrob(grob, strip_elem[1], label=expression(Y[1]))
grid.draw(grob)
